doc.title: Joanne Brackeen interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 10, 2001

title: Why players sound alike today; cycles in art
summary: She suggests innovation moves in cycles and is glad to have lived in a period of strong individual voices.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Do you think that, this is a point I was hoping to get to eventually so here we are, do you think that tendency for people to kind of sound like each other is because of the education that’s going on now or what is that about?

I’m not sure. I heard from historians that in art, there are certain periods that take place in finance, there are certain periods that take place, there’s periods where innovators are born and this goes out and moves in a certain way, and then after maybe eighty years or a © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

hundred and twenty years, whatever that cycle is, it seems to begin again. If you do a study, which I haven’t had the time but I do have the interest, in looking back at the cycles that’s hard to do though. Because our cycles now would be — the Internet and the computer are moving much differently. They are just speeded up so fast. I mean knowledge doubles every two or two and a half years, something like that. So it’s very exciting to be here now. But to answer that question, you know, there’s going to be another group. Life runs in cycles. And it’s nice to enjoy that cycle that we’re in. It’s quite amazing. But I’m glad that I was there in the cycle that I was in, there were a lot of what we call really innovators, people really seriously listening to their own voice. That comes first. The spiritual aspect, and naturistical too, coming first.
Jazz seems to move pretty fast in its development it seems like. Guys like Miles who just, when the audience catches up with him, he’s on to something else.
Um hum yeah. It works that way.
